questions.title: Stream API — Intermediate and Terminal Operations
questions.question: How does the Java Stream API work and what are the key intermediate and terminal operations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Stream: declarative pipeline for processing sequences of elements
- Lazy evaluation: intermediate operations don't execute until a terminal operation is called
- Intermediate (lazy): filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct, limit, skip, peek
- Terminal (eager): collect, forEach, reduce, count, findFirst, anyMatch, min, max
- Stream is single-use — cannot be reused after terminal operation
- Parallel streams: .parallelStream() or .parallel() — uses ForkJoinPool
- Short-circuit: findFirst, anyMatch, allMatch stop early once condition is met

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The Stream API provides a declarative way to process sequences of elements using a pipeline of operations. You describe what you want to do — filter this, transform that, collect into a list — and the stream figures out how to do it efficiently. Intermediate operations are lazy — they don't actually execute until you call a terminal operation like collect or forEach.

This laziness is important for performance. If you chain filter().map().findFirst(), the stream won't process all elements before filtering. It processes one element at a time through the pipeline and stops as soon as findFirst() finds a match — short-circuiting the rest of the pipeline.

flatMap is the operation that confuses people most. map transforms each element to another element — one-to-one. flatMap transforms each element to a stream of elements and then flattens all those streams into one — one-to-many. It's what you use when each element has a collection of sub-elements you want to iterate over: orders → order lines, departments → employees.

questions.title: Advanced Collectors and Custom Collectors
questions.question: What are the advanced Collectors operations in Java Streams and how do you write a custom collector?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Collectors.toUnmodifiableList/Set/Map (Java 10+): immutable collections
- Collectors.teeing() (Java 12+): collect into two collectors simultaneously and merge results
- Collectors.mapping(): transform before collecting in a downstream
- Collectors.counting(), summarizingInt/Long/Double for statistics
- Custom Collector: implement Collector<T, A, R> with supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher
- Collector characteristics: CONCURRENT, UNORDERED, IDENTITY_FINISH

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The Collectors class has many powerful operations beyond toList and toMap. groupingBy with a downstream collector lets you group and aggregate in one step — group employees by department and then get the average salary per department, all in one stream operation.

Collectors.teeing(), introduced in Java 12, is particularly elegant for computing two different aggregations over the same stream without iterating twice. You feed the stream into two separate collectors and provide a merge function to combine their results — for example, getting both the sum and count of a list to compute the average, or getting the min and max in one pass.

Custom collectors let you define exactly how to accumulate stream elements into your desired result. You define a supplier for the mutable container, an accumulator that adds each element, a combiner for parallel streams, and a finisher that transforms the container to the final result type.

questions.title: Stream Performance and Parallel Streams
questions.question: When should you use parallel streams and what are the pitfalls to avoid?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Parallel streams use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() — shared across the JVM
- Beneficial for: CPU-intensive, large data sets (10k+ elements), easily decomposable work
- NOT beneficial for: small datasets (parallelism overhead costs more), I/O-bound work, operations with shared mutable state
- Side effects: avoid shared mutable state — thread safety issues
- Ordering: parallel streams don't guarantee encounter order unless forEachOrdered()
- Spliterator: how streams split work — ArrayList splits well; LinkedList doesn't
- Better alternative for I/O: CompletableFuture with custom thread pool

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Parallel streams automatically split the data and process chunks concurrently using the ForkJoin common pool. They're beneficial when the operation is CPU-intensive and the dataset is large enough that the parallelism overhead is worth it — generally more than ten thousand elements and meaningful per-element computation.

The most important pitfall is using parallel streams for I/O-bound work. Making HTTP calls or database queries inside a parallel stream blocks ForkJoin worker threads, which are shared across the entire JVM. If your stream blocks all the ForkJoin threads, other things using parallel streams or CompletableFuture will stall. Use CompletableFuture with a dedicated thread pool for I/O-bound concurrent work instead.

Another pitfall is shared mutable state. If lambda functions in a parallel stream modify a shared variable — like incrementing a counter or adding to a list — you'll get race conditions. All state in parallel stream lambdas must be thread-safe or reduced using the stream's own mechanisms like reduce() or collect().

questions.title: Lambda Expressions and Functional Interfaces
questions.question: What are lambda expressions and functional interfaces in Java, and how do they work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Lambda: anonymous function — shorter syntax for implementing a functional interface
- Functional interface: interface with exactly one abstract method (@FunctionalInterface)
- Core built-in interfaces: Function<T,R>, Predicate<T>, Consumer<T>, Supplier<T>, BiFunction<T,U,R>
- Method reference: shorthand for a lambda that just calls an existing method (::)
- Closure: lambdas can capture effectively final local variables from enclosing scope
- Lambdas vs anonymous classes: lambdas don't create a new scope for 'this'
- Used as SAM (Single Abstract Method) implementations

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A lambda expression is an anonymous function that can be passed around as a value. Before Java 8, if you wanted to pass behavior to a method, you had to create an anonymous class, which was verbose. Lambdas are a shorter way to implement functional interfaces — interfaces with exactly one abstract method.

The four core functional interfaces from java.util.function cover most needs. Function takes an input and produces an output. Predicate takes an input and returns a boolean. Consumer takes an input and returns nothing — used for side effects. Supplier takes nothing and produces a value — used for lazy evaluation.

Method references are a cleaner syntax when your lambda just calls an existing method. Instead of x -> System.out.println(x), you write System.out::println. Instead of x -> x.toLowerCase(), you write String::toLowerCase. These are equivalent but more readable when the lambda body is a single method call.

questions.title: Optional — Proper Usage
questions.question: How should you use Java Optional correctly and what are the anti-patterns to avoid?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Optional: wrapper that explicitly represents the possible absence of a value — better than null
- Design intent: return type only — not for fields, not for method parameters
- Correct methods: map, flatMap, filter, ifPresent, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow
- Anti-patterns: Optional.get() without isPresent() (defeats the purpose), using Optional as field type, using Optional as parameter type
- orElse vs orElseGet: orElse always evaluates its argument; orElseGet is lazy (only if empty)
- isEmpty() and isPresent() for conditional logic
- Avoid Optional<Optional<T>> — use flatMap instead

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Optional is a container that either holds a value or is empty. Its purpose is to make the absence of a value explicit in the API contract — a method that returns Optional<User> is telling callers that the user might not exist, and they must handle that case. Compare this to returning null, which callers might forget to check.

The most important usage rules are: use Optional only as a return type, never as a field type or parameter type. Optional adds overhead — it creates an object wrapping your value — and it adds no value as a field because you'd just be null-checking the Optional object itself.

The orElse vs orElseGet distinction matters for performance. orElse always evaluates its argument, even if the Optional is present. So orElse(expensiveOperation()) always calls expensiveOperation even when there's a value to return. orElseGet takes a Supplier and only evaluates it when the Optional is actually empty.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Optional is a container that either holds a value or is empty.
speakable_v2.cap: orElseGet takes a Supplier and only evaluates it when the Optional is actually empty.

questions.title: Method References and Effective Use
questions.question: What are the four types of method references in Java and how do you use them effectively?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Method reference: shorthand syntax when lambda just calls an existing method
- 4 types: static method (Class::method), instance method of particular object (obj::method), instance method of arbitrary object (Class::method on instance), constructor (Class::new)
- Works when the lambda's signature matches the method's signature
- Improves readability — use when it makes code clearer
- Equivalent to the lambda — same bytecode effect

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Method references are a shorthand syntax for lambdas that do nothing but call an existing method. They make code more readable by removing the boilerplate of an explicit parameter and call. There are four types covering all the cases you'll encounter.

Static method references are the simplest — Integer::parseInt is the same as s -> Integer.parseInt(s). Instance method references to a specific object — like logger::info — capture a specific object. Instance method references to an arbitrary instance — like String::toLowerCase — get an instance from the stream element itself. And constructor references — like ArrayList::new — create new instances.

The key is readability. Use a method reference when it makes the code clearer. When the lambda has logic beyond a single method call — wrapping, conditionals — keep it as a lambda for clarity.
